title: SR&ED Capital Equipment and Machinery Costs | Canada FAQ
description: Canadian businesses can again claim SR&ED capital equipment and machinery costs after Bill C-15 restored them. See how the claim works.
summary: Canadian businesses can again claim SR&ED capital equipment and machinery costs: Bill C-15 restored eligibility for depreciable property acquired, and lease costs first payable, after December 15, 2024. Equipment must be intended for at least 90% SR&ED use, or 90% value consumption, in Canada. Qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn the 35% credit on these costs, but only 40% is refundable.

body.text: Canadian businesses can again claim SR&ED capital equipment and machinery costs: Bill C-15 restored eligibility for depreciable property acquired, and lease costs first payable, after December 15, 2024. Equipment must be intended for at least 90% SR&ED use, or 90% value consumption, in Canada. Qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn the 35% credit on these costs, but only 40% is refundable.
Executive Overview of the Canadian R&D Tax and Innovation Architecture

Canada maintains one of the most mature, generous, and heavily audited research and development (R&D) fiscal incentive regimes in the industrialized world. At the core of this architecture is the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, a statutory entitlement governed jointly by the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates tax policy and legislative amendments, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers technical and financial compliance. Unlike discretionary grant mechanisms that depend on competitive intake windows and finite departmental budget envelopes, the SR&ED program operates as an open-ended statutory right embedded within the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) (ITA) and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945) (ITR). Any taxpayer carrying on business in Canada that incurs qualified expenditures on work meeting the statutory definition of SR&ED is legally entitled to both an immediate—or indefinitely carryforwardable—income tax deduction under Section 37 and an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA. In the 2025–2026 fiscal cycle alone, the CRA received 24,160 claims and processed 23,677, allowing $4.6 billion in federal investment tax credits, with software development accounting for 42.6% of all credits allowed.

Between late 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential legislative transformation in over a decade. Initiated through the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, expanded in the federal Budget 2025 tabled on November 4, 2025, by the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, and enacted into law when Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1) received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the federal government fundamentally restructured the economics of the SR&ED program for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. These statutory reforms doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3,000,000 directly to $6,000,000, thereby increasing the maximum annual cash refund for qualifying corporations from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Furthermore, the legislation extended eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC beyond Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) to include a newly defined class of "eligible Canadian public corporations" (ECPCs) and their 90%-owned Canadian subsidiaries. To prevent growing technology companies from prematurely losing access to enhanced credits, the reforms widened the taxable capital phase-out thresholds for CCPCs from the historical $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million, while introducing a parallel $15 million–$75 million three-year average gross revenue phase-out test for ECPCs and permitting CCPCs to elect into the gross revenue test where advantageous. The enactment of Bill C-15 also restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and lease costs for depreciable property acquired, or lease payments first becoming payable, after December 15, 2024, reversing the decade-long exclusion of capital assets that had been enacted in 2014. Complementing these statutory enhancements, the CRA introduced an optional upfront Pre-Claim Approval process effective April 1, 2026, alongside a 90-day service standard, instead of the usual 180 days, for refundable claims selected for review that include only projects granted pre-claim approval.

Simultaneously, provincial and territorial governments have recalibrated their sub-national R&D tax incentives in response to evolving industrial priorities and federal modernization. Most notably, Quebec's 2025–2026 Budget abolished its fragmented suite of legacy R&D salary, university, and consortium tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating them into the unified, fully refundable Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation (CRIC), which offers a 30% credit on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization spend (including capital equipment) and 20% on the excess. Quebec also replaced its e-business IT salary credit (CDAE) with an artificial-intelligence-focused credit (CDAEIA) for fiscal years beginning after December 31, 2025. Concurrently, British Columbia's Budget 2026 aligned its credit with the federal reforms, doubling its refundable expenditure limit to $6 million, restoring capital expenditures, extending refundability to ECPCs, and making its provincial credit permanent, while Saskatchewan doubled its refundable CCPC expenditure ceiling to $2 million for tax years beginning after December 15, 2024. Conversely, Alberta amended its Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) rules to explicitly exclude capital expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, creating a critical federal-provincial divergence that tax auditors and corporate controllers must navigate carefully.
Federal Statutory Framework and the 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms
Section 37 Deductible Expenditure Pool and Carryforward Mechanics

The federal SR&ED regime delivers a two-pronged fiscal benefit comprising an income tax deduction under Section 37 of the ITA and an investment tax credit under Sections 127 and 127.1. Under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool all qualifying current expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a) and—for property acquired after December 15, 2024—qualifying capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) incurred in the taxation year on SR&ED carried on in Canada. Unlike ordinary business deductions governed by Sections 9, 18, and 20 of the ITA, which must be claimed in the year incurred and, if creating a non-capital loss, are subject to a 20-year carryforward expiry under paragraph 111(1)(a), the Section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool operates as an indefinite discretionary account. A taxpayer may deduct any portion of its available Section 37 pool in computing its income from a business for the current taxation year, or defer the deduction indefinitely to future taxation years without statutory expiration, subject to change-of-control loss-streaming restrictions when an acquisition of control occurs.

The balance of the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool at the end of any taxation year is dynamically adjusted through specific statutory additions and deductions. On the additions side, the pool is increased by current expenditures on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(a) and subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), restored capital expenditures on depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, under paragraph 37(1)(b), permissible foreign SR&ED salaries capped at 10% of Canadian SR&ED salaries under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), and repayments of government or non-government assistance previously deducted from the pool under paragraph 37(1)(c). On the deductions side, paragraph 37(1)(d) mandates that the pool be reduced by all amounts of government assistance—including provincial R&D tax credits and direct innovation grants—and non-government assistance, as defined in subsection 127(9), that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year. The pool is further reduced by the federal SR&ED ITC claimed or refunded in the immediately preceding taxation year as well as the amount deducted by the taxpayer in computing business income in the preceding year. Because the federal SR&ED ITC claimed or refunded in a given taxation year reduces the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year—or is included directly in business income if the Section 37 pool is driven negative—the federal ITC is effectively recaptured into corporate taxable income in the following taxation year.
Section 127 and Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credit Architecture

While Section 37 governs the deductibility of R&D outlays against taxable income, Section 127 governs the calculation and application of the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit, and Section 127.1 governs its cash refundability. Under subsection 127(5), a taxpayer may deduct its available SR&ED ITC to reduce to nil its federal Part I tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year. Any unused non-refundable SR&ED ITC earned in a taxation year may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years to offset federal Part I tax payable in those periods. Under subsection 127.1(3), any portion of an SR&ED ITC that is refunded in cash to the taxpayer in a taxation year is deemed to have been deducted under subsection 127(5) against Part I tax otherwise payable, thereby extinguishing that credit from the carryforward and carryback pools.

The federal SR&ED ITC is computed on the taxpayer's "qualified expenditures," as defined in subsection 127(9), using a two-tier statutory rate structure comprising a 15% basic rate and a 35% enhanced rate. Under the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), the baseline federal rate is 15%. This 15% basic rate applies to all qualified expenditures of corporations that are neither qualifying CCPCs nor qualifying ECPCs, such as foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries or large public corporations exceeding the gross revenue phase-out ceiling. The 15% rate also applies to qualified expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their available annual expenditure limit for the taxation year, as well as to sole proprietorships (individuals), beneficiaries of trusts, and partners of partnerships. In the case of partnerships, a partnership is not a corporation and does not claim ITCs at the entity level; rather, its SR&ED expenditures and ITCs flow through and are allocated to the partners according to their reasonable partnership shares, meaning the applicable credit rate and refundability are answered at the partner level rather than the partnership level. Conversely, under subsection 127(10.1), an additional 20% credit is added to the 15% basic credit—resulting in a combined enhanced rate of 35%—for qualifying CCPCs and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, qualifying ECPCs on qualified expenditures up to the corporation's annual "expenditure limit".
The Bill C-15 Reforms: Expenditure Limits, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations, and Phase-Out Mechanics

The enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1) on March 26, 2026, codified sweeping amendments to subsections 127(9), 127(10.1), 127(10.2), 127(10.21), 127(10.31), 127(10.32), 127(10.6), 127(10.62), and Section 127.1 of the ITA, retroactive to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024.
Expansion to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Historically, a Canadian startup that executed an initial public offering (IPO) or reverse takeover (RTO) on a designated stock exchange immediately lost its status as a CCPC under subsection 125(7), causing its federal SR&ED rate to drop precipitously from a 35% refundable credit to a 15% non-refundable credit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, subsection 127(9) introduces the statutory definition of an "eligible Canadian public corporation" (ECPC) (société publique canadienne admissible). To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must satisfy four cumulative statutory conditions under paragraph (a) of the definition in subsection 127(9), or qualify as an "eligible subsidiary" under paragraph (b). First, under subparagraph (a)(i), the corporation must be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year. Second, under subparagraph (a)(ii), the corporation must be a public corporation—having a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada or internationally, if paragraph (a) of the definition of "public corporation" in subsection 89(1) were read as "designated stock exchange"—or have elected or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue to be a public corporation. Third, under subparagraph (a)(iii), the corporation must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. Fourth, under subparagraph (a)(iv), the corporation must satisfy a hypothetical non-resident share aggregation test: even in the absence of actual knowledge of concerted control, the corporation must not be in a position where, if each share of its capital stock owned by a non-resident person—as determined based on publicly available information, including information filed pursuant to applicable securities laws before the year—were owned by a single particular person, the corporation would be controlled by that particular person. Finally, under paragraph (b) of the definition, a Canadian-resident subsidiary also qualifies as an ECPC ("eligible subsidiary") if not less than 90% (all or substantially all) of the issued shares of each class of its capital stock are owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more corporations that are qualifying ECPCs under paragraph (a).
Mathematical Formulation of the Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Regimes

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the maximum baseline expenditure limit for both CCPCs and ECPCs is doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000. However, the mechanism by which this $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out depends on whether the claimant uses the Taxable Capital Phase-Out Structure—which remains the default for CCPCs under amended subsection 127(10.2)—or the Gross Revenue Phase-Out Structure, which is mandatory for ECPCs under subsection 127(10.6) and elective for CCPCs under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32).

Under amended subsection 127(10.2), the annual expenditure limit for a stand-alone CCPC, or an associated group of CCPCs prior to allocation under subsection 127(10.21), that does not elect into the gross revenue test is determined by the statutory formula:

In this statutory equation, variable A represents the taxable capital phase-out reduction defined under paragraphs 127(10.2)(a) and (b). Variable A is nil ($0) if the taxable capital employed in Canada, within the meaning assigned by section 181.2 or 181.3 of the ITA, of the particular corporation—or the total taxable capital employed in Canada of all associated corporations—for its immediately preceding taxation year is less than or equal to $15,000,000. In any other case, variable A is equal to the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, expressed mathematically as A = min($60,000,000, Taxable Capitalprior year − $15,000,000). Consequently, for every $10 of taxable capital employed in Canada above $15,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced by $1, phasing out linearly until it reaches nil when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada reaches $75,000,000. By contrast, for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the statutory formula was $3,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A was the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $10,000,000 up to a $40,000,000 cap, which eliminated the expenditure limit entirely at $50,000,000 of taxable capital.

For an ECPC governed by subsection 127(10.6)—or for a single CCPC electing under subsection 127(10.31) or an associated group of CCPCs electing under subsection 127(10.32)—the expenditure limit is computed using the identical mathematical structure, except that the phase-out variable is based on three-year average annual gross revenue rather than taxable capital:
Expenditure LimitRevenue = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − R) ÷ $60,000,000

Under this gross revenue phase-out formula, variable R is nil ($0) if the corporation's average annual revenue over the period of three fiscal years immediately preceding and ending before the particular taxation year—based on the amounts reflected in its financial statements if not a member of a consolidated group, or reflected in the consolidated financial statements as defined in subsection 233.8(1) if the corporation is a member of a consolidated group under subsection 127(10.62)—is less than or equal to $15,000,000. In any other case, variable R is equal to the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that three-year average annual gross revenue exceeds $15,000,000, expressed as R = min($60,000,000, Average Gross Revenue3-yr − $15,000,000), which reduces the expenditure limit linearly by $1 for every $10 of average gross revenue above $15,000,000 until it is extinguished at $75,000,000.

This elective bifurcation creates a major strategic planning opportunity for capital-intensive CCPCs—such as biotechnology, life sciences, hardware, and clean-technology enterprises—that have raised substantial equity or debt financing. Because equity share capital, retained earnings, and certain debt instruments inflate "taxable capital employed in Canada" under section 181.2, a CCPC with $45 million of preceding-year taxable capital in Canada, $40 million of average gross revenue over the preceding three fiscal years, and $4.5 million of qualified current R&D expenditures would have had its expenditure limit reduced to just $375,000 under the pre-December 16, 2024 rules (generating $131,250 of refundable credits at 35% and $618,750 of non-refundable credits at 15%, for a total federal credit of $750,000). Under the enacted post-December 15, 2024 rules, that same CCPC's expenditure limit increases to $3.5 million if it elects the gross revenue test under subsection 127(10.31) ($3 million under the default taxable capital test), raising its total federal tax credits to $1.375 million ($1.225 million in refundable tax credits at 35% and $150,000 in non-refundable tax credits at 15%). Even more dramatically, a pre-revenue CCPC that raises $60 million in venture equity (pushing its taxable capital to $60 million while its three-year average gross revenue remains below $15 million) can file the revenue election under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) to preserve its full $6,000,000 expenditure limit and $2,100,000 annual refundable credit. Conversely, a mature, high-revenue software CCPC with $50 million in average gross revenue but a lean balance sheet of only $12 million in taxable capital employed in Canada can remain on the default subsection 127(10.2) taxable capital test at line 398 of Form T661 to retain its full $6,000,000 expenditure limit.

body.text: Associated Corporations, Deemed Non-Association, and Short Taxation Years

Where two or more CCPCs are "associated" with each other in a taxation year within the meaning of subsection 256(1) of the ITA, they do not each receive a separate $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Under subsection 127(10.21) and subsection 127(10.3), the associated group must calculate a single group expenditure limit—aggregating the taxable capital employed in Canada of all associated corporations for their last taxation years ending in the preceding calendar year, or aggregating consolidated group revenue if electing under subsection 127(10.32)—and allocate that limit among the associated members using prescribed Schedule 49 (T2SCH49) (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). If the associated corporations fail to file an agreement, the Minister of National Revenue is empowered under subsection 127(10.4) to allocate the expenditure limit among them. Similarly, under subsections 127.1(2.2) and 127.1(2.3), associated CCPCs are governed by group rules for refundable investment tax credits. For ECPCs that are members of a consolidated group as defined in reference to subsection 233.8(1), subsection 127(10.62) applies parallel group allocation and revenue aggregation rules.

However, the ITA contains a vital statutory relief mechanism for venture-backed corporations that become technically associated solely due to common institutional or angel investors: subsections 127(10.22) and 127(10.23), which govern the deemed non-association of corporations. Under these relieving provisions, two corporations that would otherwise be associated under subsection 256(1) are deemed not to be associated for the purposes of calculating the SR&ED expenditure limit and refundability if three cumulative conditions are met: first, one corporation is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by the other corporation; second, there is at least one shareholder of one of the corporations who is not a shareholder of the other corporation; and third, the existence of one or more shareholders of one of the corporations who is not a shareholder of the other corporation is not for the purpose of satisfying these relieving provisions, nor is the separate existence of the corporations mainly for the purpose of multiplying the SR&ED expenditure limit.

Additionally, under subsection 127(10.5), if a corporation has a short taxation year of fewer than 365 days—such as upon incorporation, amalgamation, or an acquisition of control—its expenditure limit is prorated by multiplying the otherwise determined expenditure limit by the ratio of the number of days in the short taxation year to 365. Subsection 127(10.5) also prescribes specialized proration rules where a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC having a taxation year ending in that same calendar year.
Scientific and Technological Eligibility: Statutory Definitions and Jurisprudence
Statutory Definition under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

Regardless of a claimant's corporate structure or accounting sophistication, no expenditure can enter the Section 37 pool or earn a Section 127 ITC unless the underlying activity satisfies the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls into one of three core categories under paragraphs (a), (b), or (c), or constitutes directly commensurate supporting work under paragraph (d). Basic research, defined in paragraph 248(1)(a), encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Applied research, defined in paragraph 248(1)(b), covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Experimental development, defined in paragraph 248(1)(c), comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto, and accounts for the vast majority of commercial SME claims in Canada. Furthermore, paragraph 248(1)(d) extends eligibility to supporting work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Crucially, supporting work on its own never meets the definition of SR&ED; it qualifies only to the extent that its volume and nature are strictly necessary to execute the experiments or analyses of an eligible core project.

Conversely, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes several commercial and routine technical activities from the definition of SR&ED, even when performed by highly qualified scientists or engineers. These statutory exclusions bar claims for work related to market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.
Judicial Precedents and the Five Criteria of Northwest Hydraulic

The statutory language of subsection 248(1) is interpreted and enforced through a well-settled body of Canadian tax jurisprudence. The foundational judicial authority is the decision of Justice Donald Bowman (as he then was) of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC). In Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Bowman articulated the canonical five-question test that both the CRA and the courts routinely apply to determine whether a project constitutes eligible SR&ED, requiring that all five questions be answered in the affirmative.

First, the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedure. If the resolution of the problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures or routine engineering known to competent professionals in the field, there is no technological uncertainty; genuine uncertainty arises only when it is uncertain whether an objective can be achieved at all or when system-level constraints and architectural trade-offs make the pathway unpredictable without experimentation. Second, the court examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty, requiring a conscious, structured cognitive process that identifies the specific limitation in current technology and posits a testable proposition. Third, the inquiry evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses, which distinguishes systematic experimental investigation from unguided trial-and-error tinkering. Fourth, the court determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement—meaning new knowledge that advances the taxpayer's understanding of the underlying technology rather than mere commercial novelty. Importantly, Northwest Hydraulic established that a failed experiment still qualifies as SR&ED, because proving through systematic testing that a hypothesized technological approach cannot work under given constraints advances technological knowledge by ruling out a plausible avenue. Fifth, the court asks whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed, making contemporaneous documentation an essential evidentiary pillar of the scientific method.

Although the CRA reorganized its administrative guidance by archiving its older Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy and replacing it with guidelines framed around two overarching requirements—the "Why" requirement (achieving a scientific or technological advancement) and the "How" requirement (conducting a systematic investigation by experiment or analysis)—the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, definitively confirmed that the proper legal interpretation of subsection 248(1) remains the five-question framework set out in Northwest Hydraulic.

Subsequent decisions of the Tax Court of Canada have sharpened the application of the Northwest Hydraulic test during audit disputes. In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, the appellant contested the CRA's refusal of its SR&ED projects involving custom theatrical rigging systems, and Justice Sommerfeldt of the TCC sided with the Minister, drawing a strict boundary between technical complexity and technological uncertainty. The Court held that to constitute SR&ED, a project must address a technological uncertainty that cannot be resolved by routine engineering; even when custom design work is highly complex, if competent engineers can resolve the challenges using existing knowledge and standard procedures, the work is ineligible. Similarly, in Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, the TCC ruled against the taxpayer and denied the appeal where the claimant lacked reliable contemporaneous documentation of the hypotheses tested and results obtained as the work progressed. By contrast, in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313, the TCC ruled in favour of the taxpayer regarding shop-floor SR&ED on packaging lines, demonstrating that industrial trials qualify when supported by credible evidence of systematic experimentation. Furthermore, recent TCC jurisprudence—such as Justice Bodie's ruling involving experiments to control microbial growth in a room-temperature shelf-stable vinegar-based beverage—has confirmed that a technological uncertainty can be established even where publicly available preservatives or solutions are known to competent professionals, provided those solutions have never been applied in the specific context and constraints faced by the claimant and the claimant kept sufficient contemporaneous records of the hypotheses tested and results obtained.

body.text: Software Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, and Cloud Architecture Eligibility

Because software development accounted for 42.6% of all federal SR&ED credits allowed in 2025–2026, the CRA's Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) apply heightened scrutiny to distinguish true computer science or software engineering R&D from routine commercial software development. Under CRA policy and TCC precedent, adopting off-the-shelf artificial intelligence tools, reapplying known machine learning libraries or analytical tools to new business data, routine cloud deployment, and standard API integration do not qualify for SR&ED, regardless of commercial difficulty. Conversely, software, AI, and cloud engineering qualify when developers encounter a genuine technological uncertainty—such as when it is impossible to predict whether a distributed architecture, scaling algorithm, or data synchronization process will succeed due to massive concurrency, strict latency constraints, or legacy system limitations. Qualifying work in these domains includes engineering custom orchestration or scaling algorithms supported by load-testing metrics and latency logs, migrating tightly coupled legacy monoliths to microservices where integration failure analyses and rollback logs reveal structural bottlenecks, overcoming massive concurrency and database deadlock bottlenecks through experimental sharding models, developing novel cloud security or cryptographic encryption protocols, and optimizing multi-cloud infrastructure middleware under extreme performance constraints.
Qualifying Expenditures, Overhead Calculation Methods, and Specific Cost Rules

Once a project's scientific or technological eligibility is established under subsection 248(1), the claimant must quantify its allowable Section 37 expenditures and its Section 127 "qualified expenditures" in accordance with strict statutory and regulatory accounting rules.
Salaries and Wages, the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule, and Permissible Foreign Labour

Salaries and wages represent the largest expenditure component of most Canadian SR&ED claims. Under the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, the scope of claimable employee remuneration depends on whether the claimant elects the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method or remains on the Traditional Method. If the claimant elects the Proxy Method, only the portion of salaries and wages of employees who are "directly engaged" in SR&ED in Canada may be included. Determining whether an employee is directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED is a question of fact based on how the employee's tasks correlate to the primary reason for employment; non-specialized employees may be included only if their hands-on work is directly in support of, and an integral part of, the experimental development or research and is supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications. Conversely, if the claimant uses the Traditional Method, salaries and wages for employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED may be included on the direct labour lines, and administrative salaries or wages for employees that are directly attributable (directly related and incremental) to SR&ED may also be claimed as SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661.

Across both calculation methods, strict statutory inclusion, exclusion, and payment-timing rules govern the payroll base. Claimable SR&ED salaries and wages include regular gross wages reported on a T4 slip, cash outlays for taxable benefits, and non-cash taxable benefits—provided the benefit value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs, excludes any GST/HST or PST unless no input tax credit can be claimed, and the actual costs to which the non-cash benefit relates are not also claimed as a regular business expense. Inducements and non-competition payments considered to be remuneration for services rendered during employment are also includable, as are bonuses and remuneration based on profits for employees other than specified employees. Conversely, stock option benefits are strictly excluded as they are deemed not to be an expenditure for SR&ED, and payments for extended vacation or sick leave are excluded because the employee is considered not directly engaged in SR&ED during those periods. The employer's share of related payroll benefits (such as CPP, QPP, EI, and group insurance) and retiring allowances are excluded from direct SR&ED salaries and wages, though they may be evaluated as directly attributable overhead if the Traditional Method is used. Furthermore, any salary or wages incurred in the taxation year but not actually paid within 180 days of the taxation year-end must be identified on Line 315 of Form T661 and excluded from the current year's claim; once paid in a subsequent taxation year, those amounts are claimed on Line 310 of Form T661 in that later year.

While SR&ED must generally be carried on in Canada to earn an ITC, subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA provide a narrow statutory exception for "permissible salary or wages" paid to employees carrying on SR&ED work outside Canada, which are reported on Line 307 for non-specified employees and Line 309 for specified employees, and flagged on Line 265 of Part 2 of Form T661. To qualify under subsection 37(1.4), the SR&ED work carried on outside Canada must be directly undertaken by the taxpayer, relate to a business of the taxpayer, and be solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer, and the salary or wages paid must not be subject to an income or profits tax from another country. The total permissible foreign SR&ED salary is capped at 10% of the total salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada. Separately, subsection 37(2) of the ITA permits an ordinary business income deduction—but generates no investment tax credit—for other current expenditures on SR&ED carried on outside Canada.
Specified Employees: Shareholding Thresholds, YMPE Caps, and Associated Allocations

To prevent owner-managers from artificially inflating SR&ED refundable tax credits through year-end bonuses or excessive executive compensation, the ITA and ITR impose stringent limits on "specified employees". Under the ITA and the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, a specified employee is an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the corporation or who is a "specified shareholder"—defined as a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation. For the purpose of determining this 10% shareholding threshold, shares owned by any person with whom the employee does not deal at arm's length—such as a spouse, sibling, or parent—are aggregated with the employee's own shares, and any relative of a specified shareholder is likewise classified as a specified employee.

For any individual classified as a specified employee during the taxation year, four mandatory statutory restrictions apply. First, all bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are completely excluded from claimable SR&ED salaries and wages. Second, the total SR&ED salary and wages that may be claimed for a specified employee in the Section 37 expenditure pool cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined for Canada Pension Plan purposes, prorated by the number of days in the tax year that the individual was employed, with subsection 207.8(2) of the ITA imposing a special tax where excess amounts are allocated. Third, when computing the salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the Income Tax Regulations, a specified employee's includable proxy salary base is restricted to the lesser of 75% of the employee's total salary and wages (excluding bonuses and taxable benefits) and 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year. Fourth, if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, the maximum claimable salary must be allocated among the associated corporations using prescribed Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)).
Overhead Methodologies: Prescribed Proxy Amount (55%) vs. Traditional Method

Under subsection 37(10) of the ITA and the CRA Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, a claimant must elect on Lines 160 and 162 of Form T661 whether to compute its SR&ED overhead using the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method or the Traditional Method.
The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method (ITR Subsection 2900(4))

The vast majority of Canadian SR&ED claimants elect the Proxy Method because it eliminates the administrative burden of specifically identifying, tracking, and substantiating individual overhead invoices. Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the Prescribed Proxy Amount is calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 as a flat 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, subject to an overall cap based on total business deductions. Under the Proxy Method, actual overhead expenses—such as office rent, utilities, employer payroll taxes, and administrative support—are deducted as regular business expenses only and are not included in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. However, the notional 55% PPA calculated on Line 502 of Form T661 forms part of "qualified SR&ED expenditures" in Part 4 for the purpose of earning the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit. Consequently, for every $100 of eligible non-specified employee salary under the Proxy Method, the qualified expenditure base becomes $155 ($100 direct salary plus $55 PPA), which at the 35% enhanced federal ITC rate generates $54.25 in refundable federal tax credits.
The Traditional Method (ITA Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) & ITR Paragraph 2900(2)(c))

If a claimant selects the Traditional Method on Form T661, it does not complete Part 5, enters "0" on Lines 355 and 502, and instead tracks and claims its actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360. Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the ITA and paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Income Tax Regulations, as explained in the CRA SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, an overhead or other expenditure is allowable under the Traditional Method only if it is "directly attributable" to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada by satisfying two cumulative tests: first, the expenditure must be directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, and second, the expenditure must be incremental, meaning it would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred.

Under the Traditional Method, qualifying overhead expenditures are included in both the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes, which can be advantageous when actual incremental overhead exceeds the 55% PPA. Expenditures claimable on Line 360 under the Traditional Method include the employer's share of related payroll benefits; administrative salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED; contract costs for work that is not itself SR&ED—such as the work of electricians, welders, or mechanics—that are directly related and incremental to performing SR&ED; travel and training; property taxes; maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment; moving expenses under subsection 62(3) and housing loss benefits under subsections 6(19) and 6(20); and retiring allowances, provided the retiring allowance is part of the employee's written employment contract, is incremental to SR&ED, and is reasonably allocated based on the employee's historical SR&ED salary and years of service. Furthermore, while cloud computing and software subscriptions are ordinary business deductions that are not eligible as physical materials and earn no separate credit under the Proxy Method, dedicated cloud computing instances (such as AWS, GCP, or Azure clusters) and data processing costs that are strictly linked, directly related, and incremental to SR&ED experimentation can be evaluated under the CRA guidelines for inclusion when properly tracked and segregated.

body.text: Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Transfers, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant contracts an arm's-length Canadian performer to carry out SR&ED on the claimant's behalf in Canada—reported on Lines 267 to 269 of Part 2 of Form T661—100% of the eligible contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible pool under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), while 80% of the eligible contract expenditure enters the "qualified expenditure" base under subsection 127(9) to earn the federal SR&ED ITC. For instance, a $120,000 invoice from an arm's-length Canadian engineering contractor enters the qualified expenditure base at $96,000. Conversely, any contract for SR&ED performed outside Canada earns no investment tax credit whatsoever. To prevent both the payer and the Canadian contractor from claiming SR&ED tax credits on the same work, subsection 127(9) defines a "contract payment" as an amount received or receivable by a performer for SR&ED performed for or on behalf of an arm's-length person resident in Canada or carrying on business in Canada, and requires the contractor to deduct that contract payment from its own qualified expenditures. Under the CRA Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy, if a payer subcontracts stand-alone support work described in paragraph 248(1)(d) to an arm's-length contractor, the work qualifies only if it is commensurate with and directly in support of core basic research, applied research, or experimental development carried on in Canada by the payer.

Where a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) party within the meaning of section 251 of the ITA, special statutory rules under subsections 127(9), 127(11.8), 127(13), and 127(15) govern the transaction. Under paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), the payer's expenditures on an SR&ED contract with a NAL performer are allowable Section 37 deductions in the payer's hands, but they are excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures and earn no ITC unless formally transferred. Simultaneously, the amount received or receivable by the NAL performer is not considered a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) and therefore does not reduce the NAL performer's own qualified SR&ED expenditures, allowing the NAL performer to claim the SR&ED expenditures and ITCs directly. Alternatively, subsections 127(13) and 127(15) permit the NAL performer to transfer all or a portion of its qualified SR&ED expenditures in the year—up to a maximum of the contract amount—to the NAL payer by filing an agreement on prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to transfer qualified expenditures incurred in respect of SR&ED contracts between persons not dealing at arm's length), while prescribed Form T1145 is used to allocate assistance between NAL parties. Furthermore, under subsection 127(11.8), where a taxpayer incurs an expenditure for a service or property acquired from a NAL supplier for SR&ED, the amount of the qualified expenditure and capital cost to the taxpayer are capped at the actual cost incurred by the NAL supplier. Separately, payments made to approved universities, colleges, or research institutes for SR&ED in Canada are reported as third-party payments on prescribed Form T1263 and are included in qualified expenditures at 80% for ITC purposes.
Materials Consumed or Transformed, Restored Capital Expenditures, and ITC Recapture

Physical and tangible materials used directly in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada are 100% includable in both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure base if they are either "materials consumed" (rendered virtually valueless or destroyed during experimental trials) or "materials transformed" (integrated into an experimental prototype or pilot plant that retains some value).

Following a ten-year hiatus that began in 2014, the Bill C-15 reforms restored the SR&ED eligibility of capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127(9) for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024), as well as SR&ED lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024. To qualify as an eligible SR&ED capital expenditure, at the time of acquisition the depreciable machinery or equipment (excluding buildings, land, goodwill, and inventory) must be intended either to be used all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life in the performance of SR&ED in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in the performance of SR&ED in Canada. If new equipment is used more than 50% of the time but less than 90% for SR&ED, it may still qualify for partial credits as first-term and second-term shared-use equipment under subsection 127(9). While qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn the 35% enhanced ITC on restored capital expenditures within their $6,000,000 expenditure limit, only 40% of the ITC earned at the 35% rate on capital expenditures is refundable in cash (an effective 14% cash refund), with the remaining 60% being non-refundable. Taxpayers can also coordinate their capital acquisitions with the immediate expensing measure enacted by Bill C-15 as part of the Productivity Super-Deduction, which allows a 100% first-year Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) write-off on eligible property in CCA Class 44 (patents and intellectual property), CCA Class 46 (data network infrastructure equipment and systems software), and CCA Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data processing equipment, computer hardware, and systems software) acquired after April 15, 2024 and available for use before 2027. The broader Productivity Mega Deduction announced by the Department of Finance on September 15, 2026, which would provide permanent immediate expensing for most depreciable property acquired on or after that date, remains a proposal.

Whenever a claimant claims the cost of a property—whether materials transformed into a prototype or restored capital equipment—as a qualified expenditure that earns an SR&ED ITC, the property is subject to the Recapture of Investment Tax Credit rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA, as detailed in the CRA Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy. Under subsection 127(27), as extended from 10 preceding years to 20 preceding taxation years by subsection 127(36), an ITC recapture is triggered and added directly to federal Part I tax payable if four cumulative conditions occur: the claimant acquired the particular property in the current tax year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years; the cost of the property was claimed as a qualified expenditure; a percentage of that cost was included in computing the claimant's ITC; and in the current taxation year the claimant converts to commercial use or disposes of the particular property or another property that incorporates it. The recaptured amount is calculated using the historical ITC rate applied to the proceeds of disposition (in an arm's-length sale) or the fair market value of the property (if converted to commercial use or sold to a NAL party), capped at the original ITC earned on the property. Parallel recapture rules apply to partnerships under subsections 127(28), 127(30), 127(31), and 127(35), and to NAL transferors under subsection 127(29) where qualified expenditures were transferred under a subsection 127(13) Form T1146 agreement and the property is subsequently sold or converted from all-or-substantially-all SR&ED use to commercial use.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Every Canadian province except Prince Edward Island, along with the Yukon Territory, provides a statutory R&D tax credit that stacks on top of the federal SR&ED program. With the exception of Quebec, which is administered by Revenu Québec in conjunction with Investissement Québec, and Alberta, which is administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance through the AT1 corporate return, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the CRA via harmonized T2 schedules.
Quebec: The 2025–2026 Consolidation into the CRIC and the CDAEIA Regime

In the Quebec Budget 2025–2026 tabled on March 25, 2025, the Ministère des Finances du Québec enacted a structural overhaul of Quebec's innovation tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. For taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025, Quebec corporations claimed the legacy Tax credit for salaries and wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7), which provided a 14% basic refundable rate or up to a 30% enhanced refundable rate for corporations with assets under $50 million. Effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec abolished six legacy fiscal measures—the tax credit for salaries and wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7), the tax credit for university research or research carried on by a public research centre or research consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6), the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1), the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03, subject to transitional relief until December 31, 2029, for pre-existing fee balances), the tax credit for technological adaptation services, and the industrial design component of the tax credit for an in-house design activity—and replaced them with the unified Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation (CRIC). Despite abolishing the standalone research contract and consortium credits, the Act respecting the sectoral parameters of certain fiscal measures was amended so that the Minister of the Economy, Innovation and Energy continues to issue recognition certificates for eligible public research centres and eligible research consortia for the purposes of the CRIC.

Under the new CRIC regime, eligible Quebec corporations and qualifying partnerships earn a 100% refundable two-tier tax credit that depends solely on the volume of spending rather than corporate asset size: 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an annual exclusion threshold, and 20% on all additional qualified expenditures above $1,000,000. The CRIC significantly broadens the eligible expenditure base to include 100% of salaries and wages for R&D and pre-commercialization staff in Quebec, 50% of arm's-length subcontractor expenses, 50% of payments to eligible universities, public research centres, and research consortia, and 100% of capital expenditures on new depreciable property (excluding buildings and land) used in R&D or pre-commercialization in Quebec. Before applying the 30% and 20% rates, the claimant must subtract an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Quebec basic personal amount ($18,571 in 2025) for each eligible employee, adjusted proportionally for the percentage of time each employee spends on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. For example, a startup with 1 full-time R&D employee in 2025 applies the $50,000 floor (since $18,571 is less than $50,000), whereas a firm with 5 full-time R&D employees has an exclusion threshold of $92,855 (5 × $18,571). Corporations claim the CRIC by filing Form RD-1029.8.CR (or RD-1029.8.CR-T) with their CO-17 return with Revenu Québec within 18 months of their fiscal year-end.

In parallel, Quebec reformed its flagship IT salary tax credit, the Crédit d'impôt pour le développement des affaires électroniques (CDAE), which is replaced by the Crédit d'impôt pour le développement des affaires électroniques intégrant l'intelligence artificielle (CDAEIA) for fiscal years starting after December 31, 2025. Administered jointly through an annual eligibility certificate from Investissement Québec and tax filings with Revenu Québec, the CDAE/CDAEIA requires a Quebec permanent establishment, at least 75% of gross revenue derived from eligible IT-sector activities, a minimum of 6 eligible employees devoting at least 75% of their time to eligible activities (excluding hardware-only sales, generic helpdesk support, internal corporate IT cost centres, and pure network infrastructure management), and—for fiscal years beginning after December 31, 2025 under the CDAEIA—the significant integration of artificial intelligence features into the corporation's products or processes. Crucially, for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2024, Quebec abolished the historical $83,333 per-employee salary ceiling and replaced it with an indexed annual per-employee exclusion threshold (indicative $18,952 in 2026, prorated by days) subtracted from each eligible employee's salary, enabling high-salaried senior software and AI engineers to generate substantially higher credits. While the total headline CDAE/CDAEIA rate remains 30% (cut in half to 15% from 2026 in certain non-arm's length or outside-Quebec outsourcing cases), the refundable and non-refundable split transitions by 1% per year from 2024 through 2028.

body.text: Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario operates three distinct R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA and claimed with the T2 corporate return. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 508, provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000, yielding up to $240,000 per year. Notably, the OITC is available to all corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario—not solely CCPCs—meaning a foreign-parented subsidiary can qualify if its associated group satisfies the size thresholds. The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit phases out when the associated group's preceding-year federal taxable income is over $500,000 and is eliminated at $800,000, or when preceding-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $25,000,000 and is eliminated at $50,000,000. Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), also claimed on Schedule 508, provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (net of any OITC and OBRITC claimed), which stacks with the OITC and is available to corporations of all sizes to offset Ontario corporate income tax payable. Because the OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC constitute government assistance that reduces the federal pool of deductible and qualified SR&ED expenditures, a corporation in a non-taxable loss position may deliver a written waiver of all or part of its non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC with its return—filed on or before 6 months after its tax year-end or on an amended return—to prevent an unusable non-refundable provincial credit from reducing its 35% cash-refundable federal SR&ED ITC. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) is a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under eligible contracts with qualifying Ontario research institutes, subject to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap allocated across an associated group.
Western Provinces: British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba

In British Columbia, the BC SR&ED Tax Credit—administered by the CRA on Form T666 and made permanent in BC Budget 2026—provides a 10% fully refundable tax credit to qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs up to their federal expenditure limit, and a 10% non-refundable tax credit to other corporations, active corporate members of partnerships, and CCPCs on expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit. Because the BC refundable expenditure limit is the expenditure limit as defined in the federal ITA, BC Budget 2026 (Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026) aligned the BC credit with Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024: the BC refundable expenditure limit increased from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (a maximum $600,000 refundable BC credit), the new $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 taxable capital phase-out thresholds apply, capital expenditures are again BC qualified expenditures, and ECPCs may claim the refundable credit.

In Alberta, Alberta Treasury Board and Finance administers the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) under sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and Information Circular IEG-1R4. Claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 (AS29) and AT1 Schedule 29 Listing (AS29List) within 15 months after the corporation's filing-due date, the IEG provides qualified corporations with an 8% refundable payment on eligible R&D spending carried out in Alberta up to the corporation's base spending level—calculated as the average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 taxation years—and an enhanced 20% refundable payment (structured in section 26.96 as the 8% credit plus a 12% incremental credit) on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the 2-year average base spending level, up to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $4,000,000 across an associated group (up to $800,000 per year). The $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit is prorated by days for short taxation years and phases out linearly under the formula ($40 million − C) ÷ $40 million for corporations with prior-year taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, cutting off entirely at $50,000,000. Crucially, while eligible Alberta expenditures generally match federal SR&ED qualified expenditures, Alberta specifically amended its rules so that eligible expenditures for the Innovation Employment Grant exclude capital expenditures made after December 15, 2024. The IEG is also subject to formulaic provincial recapture rules on Schedule 29 if property included in eligible expenditures is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use.

In Saskatchewan, the Saskatchewan Research and Development Tax Credit, administered by the CRA and claimed on Schedule 403 (reported on Line 645 of Schedule 5 for the refundable credit and Line 631 for the non-refundable credit), provides a 10% tax credit on eligible Saskatchewan SR&ED expenditures. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Saskatchewan doubled the annual limit for the 10% refundable CCPC credit from the first $1,000,000 to the first $2,000,000 of eligible expenditures (yielding up to $200,000 in cash refunds) and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures, while expenditures above $2,000,000 and those incurred by non-CCPCs earn a 10% non-refundable credit, subject to an overall combined annual cap of $1,000,000 in refundable and non-refundable credits. In Manitoba, the Manitoba Research and Development Tax Credit, administered by the CRA on Schedule 380 (T2SCH380), provides a 15% tax credit on eligible expenditures made in Manitoba; for in-house R&D, one-half (7.5%) is refundable and the remaining 7.5% is non-refundable, whereas R&D conducted under contract with a qualifying Manitoba post-secondary or research institution is 100% refundable at the full 15% rate.
Atlantic Canada and the Northern Territories

Three of the four Atlantic provinces—along with the Yukon Territory—provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit administered by the CRA with no corporate size tests and no annual expenditure caps. In Nova Scotia, under subsection 41(1) of the Nova Scotia Income Tax Act, corporations with a permanent establishment in Nova Scotia claim a 15% fully refundable tax credit on Schedule 340 (T2SCH340, entered on Line 566 of Schedule 5) no later than 18 months after the corporation's tax year-end, subject to a four-year provincial recapture rule entered on Line 221 of Schedule 5. In New Brunswick, corporations with a permanent establishment in the province claim a 15% fully refundable tax credit on Schedule 360 (T2SCH360), with any recapture reported on Schedule 366 (T2SCH366). In Newfoundland and Labrador, corporations claim a 15% fully refundable tax credit on Schedule 301 (T2SCH301, entered on Line 520 of Schedule 5) within 12 months after the T2 filing-due date, while individuals, trusts, and partnership members claim the credit on Form T1129. Conversely, Prince Edward Island does not have a provincial R&D tax credit program in place. In Northern Canada, Yukon is the only territory offering an R&D tax credit: claimed within 12 months of the filing-due date on Schedule 442 (T2SCH442) by corporations or Form T1232 by individuals, the Yukon Research and Development Tax Credit provides a 15% fully refundable credit on eligible Yukon SR&ED expenditures, plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on eligible expenditures paid or payable to Yukon University (formerly Yukon College), whereas the Northwest Territories and Nunavut have no territorial R&D tax credit.

body.text: Direct Innovation Grants, Government Assistance, and Stacking Mechanics
Federal Grant Ecosystem: NRC IRAP, Strategic Response Fund, and ISC/IDEaS

Beyond retroactive tax credits, Canada operates a suite of prospective direct funding programs that require pre-approval prior to incurring project costs. The cornerstone federal direct grant mechanism for small and medium-sized enterprises is the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which reaches roughly 22,500 companies annually through its Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) and provides non-repayable contributions to approximately 3,360 firms per year. NRC IRAP reimburses up to 80% of eligible internal R&D technical labour costs and up to 50% of eligible subcontractor costs; while the median IRAP award is approximately $75,000, multi-year project contributions of up to $1,000,000 are typical and a $10,000,000 ceiling exists for major projects. Furthermore, following federal governance consolidation, Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC) was wound into the National Research Council and no longer runs a separate intake; clean-technology R&D and demonstration applicants now apply directly through NRC IRAP Clean Technology.

At the large-enterprise scale, the former Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) has been renamed the Strategic Response Fund (SRF), operating with a $10,000,000 minimum contribution threshold, a mandatory consultation prior to submitting any Statement of Interest, and a structure based on repayable contributions rather than SME grants. Other targeted federal innovation vehicles include the Department of National Defence's IDEaS (Innovation for Defence Excellence and Security) program offering up to $1,500,000 per project, ISED's AI Compute Challenge, and the Scale AI Supercluster, whereas Innovative Solutions Canada (ISC) experienced a $70,000,000 annual budget reduction starting in 2025–2026 and the Canada Digital Adoption Program (CDAP) wound down permanently in 2025 with no federal micro-grant replacement.
Statutory Assistance Reduction Rules and Multi-Program Stacking Mathematics

Combining direct government grants such as NRC IRAP with provincial R&D tax credits and the federal SR&ED ITC is standard practice across Canada, subject to a ceiling of 75% total government assistance on eligible project costs under NRC IRAP stacking rules (and up to 80% under specific Quebec programs such as ESSOR and Programme DÉPART). Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, any government assistance—including NRC IRAP reimbursements and provincial R&D tax credits—or non-government assistance that a taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at its filing-due date must be deducted from the Section 37 expenditure pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure base.

However, a vital regulatory interaction creates substantial financial leverage when stacking NRC IRAP with the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method. Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount is computed on the unreduced eligible SR&ED salary base prior to subtracting the NRC IRAP grant; only after the 55% PPA is added to gross eligible expenditures is the IRAP government assistance deducted to determine net qualified expenditures for provincial and federal ITC purposes. For example, if an Ontario CCPC incurs $100,000 in eligible non-specified R&D salary and waives the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC, under Scenario A (without IRAP) its gross qualified expenditure base with the 55% PPA is $155,000, earning $12,400 in refundable Ontario OITC (8% of $155,000) and $49,910 in refundable federal SR&ED ITC (35% of the net $142,600 base), for a combined cash refund of $62,310 (62.31% of direct salary; or $65,554.15 total credits if the $4,991 non-refundable ORDTC is also claimed). Under Scenario B, if that same Ontario CCPC receives a 50% NRC IRAP grant ($50,000) on the $100,000 salary, its 55% PPA remains $55,000, yielding $155,000 in gross expenditures minus the $50,000 IRAP grant for a net provincial base of $105,000; this generates an $8,400 OITC refund (8% of $105,000) and a $33,810 federal SR&ED refund (35% of the remaining $96,600 base), bringing total combined cash recovery to $92,210 ($50,000 IRAP + $8,400 OITC + $33,810 federal SR&ED), or 92.21% of the direct salary outlay.

body.text: Compliance, Filing Procedures, Audit Defence, and Risk Governance
Statutory Filing Deadlines, Prescribed Forms, and the Subsection 162(5.1) Penalty

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the ITA, as set out in the CRA SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, a claimant must submit prescribed Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) for corporations, or Form T2038(IND) for individuals, containing all prescribed information on or before its statutory SR&ED reporting deadline. The reporting deadline is defined as 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year: for corporations, whose T2 filing-due date is 6 months after the taxation year-end, this creates an absolute deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for example, a December 31, 2024 tax year-end must file by June 30, 2026), whereas for individuals the deadline is 17.5 months after the end of the tax year. There is no statutory mechanism in the ITA to extend the subsection 37(11) reporting deadline; missing the 18-month cutoff results in the permanent disallowance of the claimed expenditures as SR&ED.

Within Form T661, claimants must file a separate Part 2 (Project Data) for each SR&ED project claimed, prepared by personnel directly familiar with the scientific or technical content of the work. Section B of Part 2 requires concise technical narratives across three prescribed fields: Line 242, which describes the scientific or technological uncertainties attempted to be overcome; Line 244, which details the systematic experimental or analytical work performed during the taxation year to overcome the uncertainties described on Line 242; and Line 246, which explains the scientific or technological advancements achieved or attempted as a result of the work described on Line 244. Part 2 also requires identifying key technical personnel and their qualifications on Lines 260 and 261, indicating whether SR&ED was performed outside Canada on Line 265, reporting whether work was carried out on behalf of another party on Line 266, listing contractors on Lines 267 to 269, and completing the contemporaneous evidence checklist. Furthermore, in Part 9 (Claim preparer information) of Form T661, all claimants who engage a claim preparer must disclose prescribed details including the preparer's name, Business Number or Social Insurance Number (collected pursuant to section 237 of the ITA), fee structure, and total compensation. Under subsection 162(5.1) of the ITA, if required claim preparer information in Part 9 is incomplete, inaccurate, or missing, the taxpayer and the claim preparer are jointly and severally liable for a strict $1,000 statutory penalty.
CRA Review Workflow, Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Defence Protocols

As part of the federal administrative modernization of the SR&ED program, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026, enabling businesses to obtain an upfront eligibility determination from the CRA within 8 weeks before incurring SR&ED costs. Under the CRA's service standards, claims accepted as filed are processed within 60 calendar days of receipt of a complete claim and refundable claims selected for review within 180 days, reduced to 90 days where the claim includes only projects granted pre-claim approval; 91% of SR&ED claims processed in 2023–2024 were accepted as filed.

When Form T661 is submitted, the CRA tax centre ingests the filing into CORTAX (or Integras for T1 claims) and routes it to the Audit Information Management System (AIMS), where field office staff conduct risk assessments and initiate coordinated technical and financial reviews. During an audit, a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) evaluates technical eligibility under the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors (RTA) against the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria, while a Financial Reviewer verifies payroll records, subsection 78(4) 180-day payment compliance, specified employee caps, contractor Statements of Work, and assistance reductions. To ensure robust audit defence, claimants must maintain a contemporaneous evidence trail—such as version-control commit logs, sprint tickets, benchmark comparisons, rollback logs, and test protocols—that records what technological uncertainty was addressed, what variables were changed versus held constant, what metrics were measured, how decisions pivoted based on test results, and who performed the work and when. If a dispute persists following an RTA and Financial Reviewer examination, the claimant may escalate concerns to the SR&ED Review Manager and, if a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued denying the claim, file a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days under subsection 165(1) of the ITA, followed by a judicial appeal to the Tax Court of Canada within the statutory timeline of subsection 169(1) of the ITA.
